transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

Well, I came in because I just keep getting these awful, unwanted thoughts. It's... it's this constant feeling that I’ve missed something critical. Like, at work, I'll be convinced I left a wrong number in a data release. Or at home, it’ll be about an unlocked back door, or maybe a bill I paid from the wrong account. And the hardest part is, even when I know I checked it, my mind just won’t let go of the possibility that I’ve caused some sort of massive disaster. It's really becoming too much to handle.
When these thoughts come up, what do you do to try to reduce the anxiety or make sure nothing is wrong?

To try and calm myself down, I end up... well, I reopen the spreadsheets I was working on. I'll reread my emails line by line just to be absolutely sure. And with things at home, I check the locks and the payment confirmations over and over. I actually have a set order I check them in, and I have to keep doing it until it finally feels safe to me. It takes up so much time. Some nights I’m still sitting at my desk hours later, and I haven't actually finished a single thing.

When you are not checking, do you worry excessively about many different ordinary areas of your life, or are the worries mainly about the specific mistakes or dangers that you feel compelled to check?

It's really just about those specific mistakes. I don't think I worry excessively about life in general, or... you know, ordinary everyday things. 

It's always tied directly to the things I feel like I have to check. Like, if I'm not obsessing over whether I corrupted a data set at work or left the house vulnerable, I'm actually fine. The anxiety is entirely focused on those specific dangers I mentioned. It's just that... well, those specific fears take up so much of my day now that there isn't really room for much else.
Do you recognize that these thoughts and checking behaviors are excessive or unreasonable, even though you feel unable to stop them?

Yes, I do. I know it doesn't make any sense to check a spreadsheet ten times when I already know the numbers are right. Or the locks—I mean, I know I locked the door the first time. It's completely unreasonable to spend hours doing it over and over. But knowing that doesn't stop the feeling. I just... I can't seem to stop myself from doing it anyway.
Which takes up more of your time and causes more distress: the unwanted thoughts themselves, or the repeated checking you do to reduce the anxiety?

I... I'm not really sure how to separate the two, to be honest. 

The thoughts are what start the panic, and they're always in the back of my head, but then the checking is what actually eats up hours of my evening. I haven't really noticed which one causes more distress or takes up more time overall. They just kind of blur together into one big cycle. So... yeah, I don't really have a clear answer for which one is worse. They both just take over my day.
If you could somehow stop the checking, how much of your day would the unwanted thoughts and doubts still occupy?

If I couldn't check... I mean, the thoughts would still be there constantly. That's actually why I came in to see you. I just keep getting these awful, unwanted thoughts that I've missed something critical. 

It's always this nagging doubt—like I put a wrong number in a data release at work, or I left the back door unlocked, or I paid a bill from the wrong account. And even when I know I already checked it, or if I forced myself not to check, my mind just won't let go of the possibility that I've caused some kind of disaster. So, if I couldn't check, those thoughts would just... they would probably occupy my mind all day.
When these doubts arise, do you usually perform the checking ritual in response to them?

Yes, I always do. To calm myself down, I... I end up reopening the spreadsheets, rereading emails line by line just to be sure. At home, it's checking the locks and the payment confirmations over and over. I have to do it in a set order until it finally feels safe. It gets so bad that some nights I’m still sitting at my desk hours later, and I haven't actually finished anything.
